Plus de deux mois se sont écoulés depuis: More than two months have passed since Canada permanently closed Roxham Road.

Plus de deux mois se sont écoulés depuis: More than two months have passed since Canada permanently closed Roxham Road. Despite this new reality, many migrants are still living in hotels, not only in Montréal but also in Ontario cities. Migrants from Roxham began to be transferred to that province in July 2022 to avoid a crisis in Quebec.
Il n’y a pas de chiffres exacts, mais le: There are no exact figures, but the migrants themselves have the impression that hundreds have chosen, for various reasons, to go back to the United States. Long waits for a first interview in the asylum process, the lack of work permits, difficulty renting an apartment, discrimination, language barriers and even unmet expectations are some of the reasons these people have returned to our neighbour to the south.
D’autres continuent d’attendre, dans l’e: Others keep waiting, hoping their asylum claims will be accepted, but they don’t know how much longer they can hold out. They say they live only on social assistance, that they don’t want to be a burden on Canada, and that what they want is to regularize their status so they can work and build a life in the country.
Après avoir vécu pendant un an au Tennes: After living for a year in Tennessee, in the United States, Juneisi Medina decided the best thing for her and her two children was to give up on the American dream. She needed to find a country that, although farther away, would let her obtain permanent residence more quickly. As Christmas decorations took over the streets, Juneisi boarded a bus for a 17-hour ride to New York. She travelled alone with her two children, and the three of them then took another bus to Plattsburgh before finally arriving at Roxham Road on December 12, 2022.
Sa vie de migrante a commencé bien avant: Her life as a migrant began well before that, and, like thousands of Venezuelans who have chosen to leave their country, it includes several attempts to settle elsewhere: in Peru, in Mexico and in the United States. “I decided to go to Canada because I was always seeing YouTubers on social media explaining the opportunities the country offers. I told myself it was a place where I could go and plan my life, but I never imagined the shock of being on stand-by for more than three months. And yes, it’s true that they help you financially, but it’s not enough. I was always thinking about how to bring in some income, because I couldn’t work. I didn’t have a work permit,” she tells La Converse from Nashville in a phone interview.
Juneisi est mère monoparentale. Son plus: Juneisi is a single mother. Her youngest son is three years old. To protect him and the rest of her family, she left Mexico, where she had managed to find refuge. “I fled Mexico because of the baby’s father. I filed five complaints there, but nothing happened. The complaints were about domestic violence. That’s why I first went to Nashville, where we lived for a year,” she explains.
À Nashville, la situation de la famille: In Nashville, the Medina family’s situation seemed to stabilize. Juneisi found a job, her eldest son was enrolled in school and her youngest could go to daycare. Despite this start at normalcy, the Venezuelan-born mother admits she had always dreamed of living in Canada. “I saw a country with more opportunities than the United States, especially for someone looking for papers, to be honest. So I asked myself what I was going to do with the money I was earning if I didn’t have papers. That’s what pushed me to go to Canada.”
Une fois au pays, la petite famille pass: Once in the country, the small family spent its first two days in the facilities that the Canada Border Services Agency and Immigration Canada had set up near Roxham Road. After finally reaching Montréal, Juneisi and her two children were placed in a hotel near Berri-UQAM station.
Le quotidien de la famille vénézuélienne: The Venezuelan family’s daily life began to take shape. Their days at the hotel were filled with procedures and waiting. Juneisi registered her youngest child to find a subsidized daycare she could afford once she was able to work legally. She went through the same process for her eldest son, who was supposed to start Grade 5 that year. Finally, she managed, with some difficulty, to open a bank account so she could receive the $1,194 in assistance the Quebec government gives her, and she bought a cellphone so she could communicate.
Juneisi Medina et son fils aîné dans le: Juneisi Medina and her eldest son in the Old Port of Montréal (left) and the Venezuelan woman in Nashville, where she currently lives. Photo: Pablo A. Ortiz
Après trois mois à l’hôtel, Juneisi est: After three months at the hotel, Juneisi was told she had to leave the facility or move to other accommodation near Montréal’s airport. To be able to leave, she had to find a way to rent an apartment, which she eventually managed to do, though not without difficulty. “I faced a lot of discrimination. I had to beg people. When they agreed and I told them I had two children, they told me the space was too small, and we’re talking about two-bedroom apartments. In the end, I got it because a Mexican man transferred his lease to me,” she explains.
Tout juste trois jours avant la date lim: Just three days before the deadline set by Immigration Canada authorities, Juneisi left the hotel and moved into her new apartment. She had only one mattress, which she shared with her two children for the first few days. Her eldest son then started school, which became another source of anxiety for Juneisi. According to her, he was placed directly in a regular class, without going through a welcome class, so he had to follow lessons without really understanding French. Although she tried to find other options, she couldn’t change anything. Her youngest son always stayed with her, because Juneisi couldn’t get a spot in a subsidized daycare and was unable to pay the more than $1,000 a month needed for an unsubsidized private daycare.
Le loyer de son appartement s’élevait à: The rent for her apartment was $1,000. Once that was paid, the single mother had to divide what was left between food and transportation. Despite all her efforts to find other sources of income, what she could earn wasn’t enough. That’s why she finally decided to look for cash work. She ended up cleaning at the Olympic Stadium, for a company that hires people and pays them $15 an hour. “I went twice to do cleaning. I spent 12 hours cleaning the stadium seats. We only had a 15-minute break in the morning and another in the afternoon. I left around 10 p.m.,” she says.
Un autre moyen de gagner plus d’argent a: Another way to earn more money was to rent out one of the rooms to a fellow Venezuelan, but when she reported that she had a roommate, the social assistance she was receiving went down.
Le 15 avril 2022, quatre mois et trois j: On April 15, 2022, four months and three days after taking Roxham Road, Juneisi had a conversation with her roommate that would change her fate. “My roommate told me that night that it was very hard to find a job here. I first told him I wasn’t leaving, that I had to stay because of my kids, and he answered: ‘What have you done in four months, what have you gained, what have you accomplished? You can’t even send money to your family, you can’t even go out for a walk with your kids.’ I told him he was right. I thought about it for a few minutes and at 10:30 p.m. he said: ‘Juneisi, we’re leaving today, do you want to come?’ I thought again and said: ‘Yes, let’s go.’ I quickly settled the rent with a neighbour who was looking for an apartment for her nephew. Then I took a backpack, put in a couple of small items of clothing for the kids and some shoes, and that’s how we left,” she says. They paid $300 to have someone drive them to the border.
Juneisi, ses deux enfants et son colocat: Juneisi, her two children and her Venezuelan roommate crossed into the United States through a wooded area that was nonetheless full of lights. “They’re very big lights that shine way too bright. From there, we walked about 800 m. You can’t turn on your cellphone so you don’t attract attention. Then you just keep walking until you meet the American border patrol agents. They asked us if we were coming from Canada and nothing else. They didn’t take our cellphones or anything else. Then the process of collecting our data started again, and since everything was already in the system, it was all simpler.”
Juneisi est donc retournée à Nashville,: So Juneisi went back to Nashville, Tennessee, where she already had a life, acquaintances and a job, and where her children went to school. Although living in Nashville was easier, getting papers there seemed very difficult. Today, the mother works in construction, the same sector she worked in before leaving Venezuela. Her 11-year-old son is starting Grade 6, and her youngest boy is in daycare. Barely a month after arriving in Nashville, Juneisi was able to buy a car with the money she earns from her cash work.
Depuis les États-Unis, Juneisi s’est ren: From the United States, Juneisi realized that the Quebec government was still paying her social assistance. She called an office of the Ministère de l’Emploi et de la Solidarité sociale to report that she was no longer in Canada, but so far without success. “I don’t want that money, but they haven’t stopped depositing it, and it’s something I want them to fix now,” she says.
Bien qu’elle se dise financièrement sati: Although she says she is financially satisfied with her decision to return to the United States, the mother does not rule out coming back to Canada in the future. “I’m very happy financially, but not at all psychologically. Sometimes I have regrets and I want to go back,” she says, adding that getting papers in the United States is a burdensome and expensive process. “I can’t go back now. I’ll drive my kids crazy. But I’m speaking to you from the bottom of my heart: I tell myself, my God, I went back because of the money, but honestly, when am I going to get papers here?”
Nohemí Rentería a déclaré qu’il est poss: Nohemí Rentería said it is possible that some asylum seekers found Canada’s immigration process very difficult and that others don’t seem to have really intended to stay in the country. Photo: Pablo A. Ortiz
Nohemí Rentería est une leader communaut: Nohemí Rentería is a community leader based in Niagara Falls. She has lived in Canada for 14 years and works in her field, international trade, but she also devotes her free time to working in finance and volunteering to help newly arrived migrants, including asylum seekers. Through the Christian church she attends, Nohemí learned about the situation of migrants who arrived in Canada through Roxham Road and were transferred to Ontario.
« La forte vague s’est poursuivie jusqu’: “The big wave continued until March. My colleagues and I saw many Indians, Pakistanis, Africans, Colombians, Nicaraguans and Venezuelans arrive. They were housed in hotels in Niagara Falls starting in November 2022. But it’s true that many are going back to the United States. Many did so even before Roxham closed,” she tells La Converse by phone.
Selon Nohemí, les autorités ontariennes: According to Nohemí, Ontario authorities are currently offering to transfer migrants who want to settle in other provinces of Canada. “Last month, for example, they started telling everyone they needed to start looking for housing. Some went to London because rents are cheaper there, others stayed in Niagara Falls. I know six families who have already moved, and others have gone to British Columbia and Saskatchewan,” she adds.
Et puis, il y a ceux qui ont décidé de r: And then there are those who decided to go back to the United States. “They told me it was very hard for them. In the United States, you go out and you can easily find a paid job. Plus, there are a lot of people who speak Spanish, whereas here, many migrants find it very hard to speak English. Others are deeply affected by being shut in hotels, because everything is far away. Before, they were in New York and could get around more easily. Here, they have to ask for help or walk a lot. The climate also played a role, because many arrived in the middle of winter,” says Ms. Rentería.
Pour la leader communautaire, de nombreu: For the community leader, many migrants had no intention of staying in Canada. “They simply wanted to save money and go back to their country or to the United States. They came on the recommendation of others, because some people embellish things by saying that in Canada they give you papers. What a lot of people don’t see is that it’s a sacrifice, that it takes time and, above all, that you really need to have a case to claim asylum.” There have also been cases, according to Nohemí, of people who came to the country, bought cars, maxed out their credit cards and then went back to the United States. “It’s unfortunate, because because of those few cases, migrants all get lumped together,” she laments.
Nohemí estime qu’il est possible que les: Nohemí believes it is possible that the migrants who agree to be transferred to other provinces are the ones who want to build their lives in Canada. She acknowledges, however, that a large share of asylum seekers are doing their best to stay in the country.

Pedro (nous avons modifié son prénom à s: Pedro (we changed his first name at his request) is another Venezuelan who arrived in Canada through Roxham Road. As with Juneisi, his life as a migrant began years ago, and one of his destinations was Peru.
Plus récemment, Pedro quitte le Venezuel: More recently, Pedro left Venezuela on September 11, 2022. He made the journey on foot and by car, starting in Colombia. He first crossed the Darién jungle, part of which is in Panama, then went through Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Honduras and Guatemala until he reached Mexico. He left hundreds of dollars with coyotes, the smugglers who guarantee access to irregular routes. “Sometimes even the local police make us pay. I came with borrowed money, and my goal was always to live in Canada,” he tells La Converse.
Avant d’arriver aux États-Unis, Pedro se: Before arriving in the United States, Pedro was in Juárez, Mexico, when the Biden administration declared that all irregular migrants would be sent back to Mexico. There, he managed to work and recoup part of the money he had spent on his journey.
Le 24 décembre de la même année, le jeun: On December 24 of that year, the young man took his chances and crossed the Rio Grande to enter the United States.
Une fois en terre américaine, atteindre: Once on American soil, reaching Canada became his first goal. “I first went to Denver and from there I managed to get to New York. That trip was paid for by a migrant aid association in Denver. Once in New York, I took a bus to Plattsburgh. The bus was full, we were all going to cross the border. On January 10 at 7 a.m., we arrived in Canada,” he says.
Pedro est ensuite logé dans un hôtel de: Pedro was then housed in a hotel on Berri Street, where he stayed for two months. He was then transferred to a hotel near Montréal’s airport. He stayed there only eight days before being sent to the headquarters of the Programme régional d’accueil et d’intégration des demandeurs d’asile (PRAIDA), where he stayed for two weeks. “They told me I was running out of time, so I looked for housing. On April 1, I moved to the South Shore with the money I was getting from social assistance. The reality is that this assistance isn’t enough for me; that’s why I’m thinking of going to the United States. This month will be decisive, because if nothing changes by the end of the month, I’ll have to leave again,” he says. Pointing to his clothes and his bag, he exclaims: “This is all I have.”
Le Vénézuélien raconte aussi que, dans l: The Venezuelan also says that, given his situation, he often chooses to do his grocery shopping on foot, because even paying for transportation is hard for him.
Bien qu’il ait été conseillé par un avoc: Although he was advised by an immigration lawyer, whom he preferred not to name, Pedro says he had asked for a refund of the $1,000 advance he had paid for the processing of his asylum claim, because he feels this professional did little to move his file forward. “I was in danger because of the work I did. They wanted us to support the government, which I didn’t like. I worked in a special unit. I never took part in protests,” says the young man, who was part of the Bolivarian National Police, a Venezuelan government body that Amnesty International has singled out as responsible for the repression suffered by part of the Venezuelan population during the 2017 protests. Pedro assured La Converse that he did not take part in the repression.
Pedro dit que les personnes qu’il connaî: Pedro says the people he knows who entered the country with him already have a work permit and meet the main requirements to be able to work legally. He is still waiting and sees no solution to his problem. Of the $800 in financial assistance he receives, $600 goes to rent. He has to divide the other $200 among food, transportation and his cellphone plan. Meanwhile, he has been contacting Immigration Canada, but since he speaks neither French nor English, he is told they can’t help him. “My roommate told them he could translate what I wanted to say, but they said they couldn’t accept that,” he adds, exasperated.
Le dilemme de ce jeune homme est grand,: The young man’s dilemma is enormous, because he lives alone in Canada while his whole family is in Venezuela, including his six-year-old daughter, who lives with his parents. “My parents are elderly. My mother suffers from migraines, and my father had a stroke in 2019. He’s disabled. My family depends on me.”
Pedro sait que de nombreux migrants ont: Pedro knows that many migrants turn to informal work to make ends meet. It’s a solution he has tried, but he says he fears being the victim of a scam, showing some messages sent to him by alleged labour recruiters. “All of this looks like a scam,” he says, adding that he knows migrants who worked cash, who were exploited and who weren’t paid after working.
La fatigue et l’inquiétude se lisent sur: Fatigue and worry show on the young Venezuelan’s face. He says he suffers from insomnia and prefers not to tell his parents what he is going through, so as not to worry them. In the meantime, he keeps counting the days until the deadline he has set for himself to finally know what he will do. While he waits, he takes the opportunity to send a message to immigration services: “It would be good to speed up the process for asylum seekers so they can get their work permits. That way, the government wouldn’t have to carry the burden we represent, and we would have the chance to start working. I’m not looking for a particular job. I’m willing to work in any field: construction, sweeping, cleaning, anything.”
Aucune décision n’a encore été prise, ma: No decision has been made yet, but Pedro knows exactly what going back to the United States would mean. He has been through it before, and it has made him resilient. “It would mean… starting over from zero,” the young man concludes, as these could be his last moments in the country.
